newsitem.title: USA: Localities say bankruptcy law draining them dry.
newsitem.headline: Localities say bankruptcy law draining them dry.

text.p: Tax collectors from school districts nationwide lined up Friday in support of draft federal legislation to help shield them from a U.S. bankruptcy code they warn is draining their coffers dry.
"We have accounted for $449,593 in revenue lost" from six bankruptcy cases alone, Jayne Morrell, tax collector for the Dallas Independent School District told a U.S. Senate Judiciary panel.
That is equivalent to the cost of 14 classroom teachers, 230 campus computers or $150 in additional school supplies each for 3,000 teachers, Morrell told panel chair Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa.

Grassley is circulating draft legislation to ease the impacts of bankruptcy claims on localities. One provision would move state and local property tax liens higher on the list of creditors when local companies declare bankruptcy.

"Now we're near the bottom of the list," a spokesperson for state and local governments said. "And the problem is that a lot of education dollars are allocated from property taxes, particularly in states like Texas that don't have a property tax."

Morrell also said that the city of Dallas lost $248,301 in revenue because of bankruptcy collections. "This would have funded five police officers, or 2,800 immunizations for children ages 0-2, or 150 lane-miles of street repairs," Morrell said.
Grassley said, "The current bankruptcy system is very unfair for local governments because it drains badly-needed revenue. We can't just keep doing things the old way."
